lead: Say the same thing a different way, and how we feel and choose can shift with it.
when: When you're reading promotional material, comparing options, or talking about risk, or when you notice that a different wording clearly changes how you feel.
body:
"Nine out of ten people finished" and "one out of ten people didn't finish" describe exactly the same result. But the first makes you notice success, and the second makes you focus on failure. The framing effect is about how the way something is presented shapes how we understand it.

The framing effect is the phenomenon in which the same problem, or equivalent options, lead to different judgments and choices depending on how they are presented, which aspect is emphasized, or how they are described.

We can never see information completely apart from how it's expressed. What goes in the headline, whether benefits or costs come first, whether you use head counts or percentages: each can pull attention to a different place. The problem is that we may believe we're choosing based on the full facts when we've actually seen only the side that was emphasized.

One practical habit is to restate the same information from the opposite direction: how many finished, and also how many didn't; what you'll gain, and also what you'll pay. Putting both versions side by side usually helps more than just swapping in a nicer-sounding word.

A side-by-side comparison should use the same group, the same denominator, and the same standard, changing only where the emphasis falls. That way you can see it's the angle of description that changes, not the data or conditions being quietly swapped out.
example:
One course description says: "Of last term's 100 students, 90 completed every exercise." You feel the course would be easy to stick with. Another page says: "Of last term's 100 students, 10 didn't complete every exercise." Now you start worrying you won't keep up.

If both are about the same group of people and the same definition of "completed," the two sentences don't contradict each other. First write them together as "90 completed, 10 didn't," then ask how much time the exercises take, what counts as completing them, and whether those students were in a situation like yours. It's fine to notice how the wording makes you feel, but the decision needs these concrete details.
extra:
You're planning a weekend activity and say it "takes up two hours." Your friend feels their downtime is being squeezed. Say instead that "the rest of the time is still free," and it sounds more relaxed. If the activity takes the same time either way, you've only moved the spotlight.

When you talk it over, lay out the whole plan: two hours for the activity, travel time on top, and which hours are free. The point isn't to pick the wording that wins the other person over, but to let both of you decide while looking at the same schedule.
steps: Translate the description back into concrete people, numbers, time frames, and conditions, and check first whether the two versions really are equivalent.
Restate it from the complementary angle: write down both who finished and who didn't, both the gains and the costs.
Decide based on your own goals and the full set of conditions, not just the first feeling one sentence gives you.
caution: Two statements that sound alike don't necessarily say the same thing. With "$15 a month" versus "$180 a year," you still need to check whether you must pay annually and whether you can cancel; if the conditions differ, it's more than a framing difference. The framing effect also doesn't mean every way of putting things is manipulation. Clear, complete presentation genuinely helps people understand.
exercise: Pick one description that excited or worried you. Write down the side it emphasizes and the side it leaves out. After rewording it, did the facts change? How much did your feeling change?
brief: The same plate of ten dots is highlighted through two different viewing frames: the left frame focuses on nine plain dots, the right on one brick-red dot. Two stick figures react differently, while the underlying facts stay the same.
diagramCaption: Two bars with the same total and the same split. The top one emphasizes the finished part, the bottom one the unfinished part. What stands out changes, but the underlying numbers don't.
